notes.b: Organic chemistry is the study of the compounds of carbon, and hydrocarbons are the simplest of them.
points: Carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, carbonates and hydrogencarbonates contain carbon but are classed as inorganic.
Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds and carbon atoms bond strongly to each other, giving stable chains, straight or branched, and rings of almost any length.
Organic compounds are divided into many groups, or homologous series, each with its own characteristic structure and reactions (see “Groups of hydrocarbons”).
A hydrocarbon is a compound containing carbon and hydrogen only.

Other organic families, such as alcohols and carboxylic acids, can be thought of as hydrocarbons with one or more hydrogen atoms replaced by other atoms or groups, so hydrocarbons are the basis for understanding other organic compounds.

notes.b: Crude oil, natural gas and coal are the main sources of hydrocarbons, and all three are fossil fuels.
points: Fossil fuels formed over millions of years from the remains of plants and animals, buried under sediment and changed by heat and pressure in the absence of air; crude oil and natural gas formed mainly from tiny marine organisms.
Fossil fuels are finite (non-renewable): they are being used far faster than they form.
Natural gas is mainly methane (CH₄), typically over 80%, with small amounts of ethane, propane and butane.
Crude oil is a mixture of many hydrocarbons, mostly alkanes in chain and ring form, with some aromatic hydrocarbons such as benzene.
Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation into fractions, each a mixture of hydrocarbons with a similar range of boiling points and so of similar molecular size.
The smallest molecules, with the lowest boiling points, are collected at the top of the column and the largest at the bottom (see “Separation techniques”).
Methane forms when bacteria break down plant and animal material in the absence of air, a process called anaerobic decomposition.
This methane is found in landfill sites (refuse dumps), slurry pits, marshes and the digestive systems of cattle and sheep.
Biogas, made deliberately by anaerobic digestion of farm slurry, food waste or crops, is mainly methane and is a renewable fuel.
Plants also make hydrocarbons, e.g. natural rubber, which is poly(isoprene) from the rubber tree, and limonene (C₁₀H₁₆) in citrus-fruit peel oil.
Hydrocarbons can be synthesised from other substances, e.g. ethene is made by dehydrating ethanol (see “Investigation: preparing ethene”).
Ethanol made by fermenting sugar cane gives a plant-based, or “bio”, ethene.
The Fischer–Tropsch process makes liquid hydrocarbons from carbon monoxide and hydrogen, so synthetic fuels can be made starting from coal, natural gas or biomass.

notes.b: Most hydrocarbons are burned for energy, because they release a lot of energy when they burn in oxygen.
points: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon in oxygen gives carbon dioxide and water (see “Combustion”).
Methane (natural gas) is used for heating and cooking in homes, and for generating electricity in power stations.
Propane and butane are the main components of LPG (liquefied petroleum gas), sold in cylinders for patio heaters, camping stoves, gas barbecues and some vehicles such as forklift trucks.
Small butane canisters are used in camping stoves and lighters.
Natural gas and LPG have no smell of their own, so a small amount of a strong-smelling sulfur compound, a thiol also called a mercaptan, is added so that leaks can be detected.
Liquid fractions of crude oil are transport fuels: petrol for cars, kerosene for jet aircraft and home heating oil, and diesel (gas oil) for lorries, buses, tractors and cars.
Heavy fuel oil is used in ships and furnaces.
Ethyne (acetylene) burned in pure oxygen gives a flame above 3000 °C, used for cutting and welding metals in the oxyacetylene torch.

notes.b: A smaller share of hydrocarbons is used as raw materials, or feedstocks, for the chemical industry rather than being burned.
points: Ethene and propene are made into the plastics poly(ethene) and poly(propene) (see “Addition polymers”).
Ethene is also used to make ethanol and ethane-1,2-diol, the antifreeze, and to ripen fruit, because it is a plant hormone.
Benzene is a feedstock for plastics such as polystyrene, and for detergents, dyes and pharmaceuticals.
Methane is the main source of hydrogen for making ammonia, which is used to make fertilisers.
Hexane and cyclohexane are used as non-polar solvents, e.g. hexane to extract vegetable oils from seeds.
The largest molecules give lubricating oils and greases for machinery, paraffin wax for candles, and bitumen, from the residue, for surfacing roads and waterproofing roofs.

notes.b: The size and bonding of a hydrocarbon decide which use suits it.
points: Small molecules are gases that burn easily, so they make fuels.
Unsaturated alkenes react readily, so they make feedstocks for plastics.
Large molecules are viscous or solid, so they make lubricants, waxes and bitumen.

notes.b: The investigation asks for one major impact on society of the extensive use of hydrocarbons, researched from secondary sources and judged on the evidence.
points: Choose one impact and set a focused question, often about one sector or one country.
Use several reliable sources that agree, judging each for authority, evidence, date and bias, since oil companies and campaign groups may each present one side.

Reliable sources for these topics include peer-reviewed papers and reports of the IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change), the WHO, the EPA (Environmental Protection Agency, Ireland) and the SEAI (Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland).
Explain the chemistry with balanced equations, and consider solutions and their limits.

Set every impact against the benefits: hydrocarbons are cheap, energy-dense and easily transported fuels and raw materials that made modern transport, heating, electricity, plastics and medicines possible.
Justify the conclusion from the evidence, and acknowledge uncertainty and what the sources could not show.

notes.h: Option 1: climate change, chemistry and scale
notes.b: Research question, e.g. “How does burning hydrocarbons for transport in Ireland contribute to climate change, and how could it be reduced?”
points: Complete combustion of every hydrocarbon releases carbon dioxide: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l); 2C₈H₁₈(l) + 25O₂(g) → 16CO₂(g) + 18H₂O(l).
Burning 1.00 kg of methane: 1000 g ÷ 16 g mol⁻¹ = 62.5 mol CH₄, which gives 62.5 mol CO₂ × 44 g mol⁻¹ = 2750 g, so 2.75 kg of CO₂ is released.
Burning 1.00 kg of octane: 1000 g ÷ 114 g mol⁻¹ = 8.77 mol C₈H₁₈, which gives 8.77 mol × 8 × 44 g mol⁻¹ = 3088 g, so 3.09 kg of CO₂ is released.

notes.h: Option 1: climate change, evidence and effects
points: Fossil carbon was locked away for millions of years; burning it moves that carbon into the atmosphere far faster than the carbon cycle removes it, so atmospheric CO₂ rises.
CO₂ and methane are greenhouse gases that absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth and so trap heat (see “The enhanced greenhouse effect”).
Methane escapes from gas wells, pipelines and coal mines.
Atmospheric CO₂ has risen from about 280 ppm before the Industrial Revolution to over 420 ppm today, and global average temperature has risen by more than 1 °C since pre-industrial times.
Consequences include rising sea levels, more extreme weather such as storms, floods and droughts, and ocean acidification as CO₂ dissolves: CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq).

notes.h: Option 1: climate change, solutions and limits
points: Solutions include renewable electricity from wind and solar, electric vehicles and heat pumps, energy efficiency, biofuels, hydrogen, and carbon capture and storage.
The limits of these solutions include cost, the supply of materials such as those for batteries, the intermittency of renewables, and the time needed to change infrastructure.

notes.b: Research question, e.g. “How has burning solid fuel and road fuels affected air quality and health in Irish towns?”
points: Incomplete combustion, with too little oxygen, produces carbon monoxide and soot, e.g. 2CH₄(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO(g) + 4H₂O(l).
Nitrogen and oxygen from the air combine at the high temperatures in engines: N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g); 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g).
Sulfur impurities in coal and heavy oils burn to sulfur dioxide: S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g).
Unburned hydrocarbons such as benzene, a carcinogen, are released from fuel evaporation and exhausts.

notes.h: Option 2: air quality, effects on health
points: Carbon monoxide is toxic: it binds to haemoglobin in the blood more strongly than oxygen does, reducing the blood's ability to carry oxygen.

Particulate matter, such as PM2.5 (particles with a diameter below 2.5 μm), from diesel engines and from burning coal and wood is breathed deep into the lungs and is linked to asthma, lung disease and heart disease.
Nitrogen dioxide irritates the lungs and contributes to acid rain and smog.
Sulfur dioxide irritates the airways and causes acid rain.
Dublin banned the sale of smoky (bituminous) coal in 1990; black smoke fell sharply, and later studies linked the ban to fewer deaths from respiratory and heart disease.
The ban on smoky coal was extended to the whole country in October 2022.
Catalytic converters, low-sulfur fuels, particulate filters and electric transport also reduce emissions.

notes.b: Research question, e.g. “What happens to single-use plastic packaging in Ireland, and how could its impact be reduced?”
points: Most plastics are made from hydrocarbon feedstocks: ethene and propene are polymerised to poly(ethene) and poly(propene) (see “Addition polymers”).
Addition polymers are long chains held by strong, non-polar C–C and C–H bonds, so microorganisms cannot break them down.
Plastics are non-biodegradable and can persist for hundreds of years.
Plastic waste causes litter and fills landfill sites.
Plastic in the sea entangles or is swallowed by marine animals.
Plastics break into microplastics, pieces smaller than 5 mm, which are found in water, food and living things.
Burning plastics recovers energy but releases CO₂, and burning some plastics, such as PVC (poly(chloroethene)), releases toxic gases such as hydrogen chloride unless done in controlled incinerators.

notes.h: Option 3: plastic waste, solutions and limits
points: Reducing and reusing plastics avoids the waste altogether.
Recycling involves sorting, washing, shredding, melting and remoulding, but only some plastics can be recycled and only for a limited number of cycles.
Biodegradable and bio-based plastics, deposit-return schemes, bans and levies are other responses; Ireland introduced a plastic bag levy in March 2002.

notes.h: Option 4: energy dependence, the research question
notes.b: Research question, e.g. “How does Ireland's dependence on imported oil and gas affect energy prices and security?”
points: Modern economies depend on hydrocarbons for transport, heating, electricity generation, farming, where fuel and fertiliser are made from natural gas, and plastics.
Jobs and government revenue depend on the industry.
Fossil fuels are finite and unevenly spread, so countries without their own reserves must import them and are exposed to price shocks and supply cuts.
The 1973 oil crisis was an oil embargo by Arab oil-producing countries, and in 2022 gas and electricity prices rose sharply after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
Ireland imports most of its energy.
Ireland's own natural gas has come from the Kinsale Head gas field, off Co. Cork, which stopped producing in 2020, and from the Corrib gas field off Co. Mayo.
Extraction and transport carry risks with economic costs.
Oil spills such as the Exxon Valdez (Alaska, 1989), the Prestige (off Galicia, Spain, 2002) and Deepwater Horizon (Gulf of Mexico, 2010) damaged fisheries, tourism and wildlife.

notes.h: Option 4: energy dependence, solutions and limits
points: Home-produced renewable energy, energy efficiency and electrification reduce imports.
The transition needs investment and takes time.
Hydrocarbons are still needed as feedstocks for plastics, medicines and fertilisers, so some argue they should be conserved for these uses rather than burned.
State the answer to the research question in one or two sentences.
Support the answer with the strongest evidence and the chemistry, using equations and data.
Weigh the benefits against the harms, and assess the proposed solutions for cost, practicality and who is affected.
Note the limitations of the sources used and what further research would help.

keyTerms.definition: A compound containing carbon and hydrogen only, the simplest kind of organic compound.
A compound of carbon, excluding the simple carbon oxides, carbonates and hydrogencarbonates.
A fuel, such as crude oil, natural gas or coal, formed from the buried remains of living things over millions of years.
Separation of crude oil into fractions by boiling, with each fraction collected over a narrow range of boiling points.
A mixture of hydrocarbons with a similar range of boiling points, collected during the fractional distillation of crude oil.
The breakdown of plant and animal material by bacteria in the absence of air, producing methane.
A renewable gas, mainly methane, made by anaerobic digestion of waste or crops.
A raw material used by the chemical industry to make other substances.
Liquefied petroleum gas, mainly propane and butane, stored under pressure in cylinders.
A strong-smelling sulfur compound, also called a thiol, added to natural gas and LPG so that leaks can be detected.
Burning in too little oxygen, which produces carbon monoxide and soot instead of carbon dioxide alone.
A gas, such as carbon dioxide or methane, that absorbs infrared radiation emitted by the Earth and so traps heat.
The lowering of seawater pH as carbon dioxide dissolves in the sea to form carbonic acid.
Rain made acidic by sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides reacting with water in the atmosphere.
Fine solid particles in the air, such as soot, that can be breathed deep into the lungs.
A substance that can cause cancer.
A piece of plastic smaller than 5 mm that persists in water, food and living things.
Able to be broken down by microorganisms into natural substances.
A reliable supply of energy at affordable prices.

questions.prompt: What is a hydrocarbon? Outline the three main sources of hydrocarbons, giving an example of each.
questions.model: A hydrocarbon is a compound containing carbon and hydrogen only. The three main sources are fossil fuels, living matter and synthesis. Fossil fuels: crude oil, natural gas or coal, formed from the buried remains of plants and animals over millions of years. Living matter: methane produced when bacteria break down plant and animal material in the absence of air, for example in slurry pits, or natural rubber from the rubber tree. Synthesis: ethene made by dehydrating ethanol.

questions.prompt: Give one use of each of the following and explain why the hydrocarbon suits that use: (i) methane, (ii) a mixture of propane and butane, (iii) ethene.
questions.model: (i) Methane is used for heating and cooking in homes. It is a gas that burns cleanly and can be piped to homes. (ii) Propane and butane are used as LPG in cylinders for camping stoves and patio heaters. They are easily liquefied under pressure, so a large amount of fuel can be stored in a small, portable cylinder. (iii) Ethene is used to make poly(ethene). Its C=C double bond makes it reactive, so it can be polymerised by addition.

questions.prompt: Natural gas is odourless. Explain why a sulfur compound is added to it, and name two sources of methane other than natural gas wells.
questions.model: A strong-smelling sulfur compound, a thiol or mercaptan, is added to natural gas because the gas has no smell of its own, so leaks can be detected. Two sources of methane other than natural gas wells are landfill sites (refuse dumps), slurry pits, marshes, and the digestive systems of cattle and sheep. Any two of these.

questions.prompt: Outline a research investigation into one major impact on society of the extensive use of hydrocarbons. Include your research question, two suitable sources and how you would judge them, the chemistry involved and a conclusion.
questions.model: Research question: for example, How does burning hydrocarbons for transport in Ireland contribute to climate change, and how could it be reduced? Two suitable sources: a report of the IPCC and a peer-reviewed paper, each judged for its authority, the evidence it gives, its date and any bias. Chemistry: complete combustion of octane, 2C₈H₁₈(l) + 25O₂(g) → 16CO₂(g) + 18H₂O(l), and of methane, CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), releases carbon dioxide. The carbon was locked away for millions of years, so burning it raises atmospheric CO₂, which absorbs infrared radiation and traps heat. Conclusion: state the answer in one or two sentences and support it with the evidence, such as CO₂ above 420 ppm and warming of more than 1 °C. Weigh the benefits of hydrocarbons against the harms, assess solutions such as renewable electricity and electric vehicles for cost and limits, and note the limitations of the sources used.

questions.prompt: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced when 1.00 kg of methane burns completely, and explain why this contributes to climate change.
questions.model: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). Moles CH₄ = 1000 g ÷ 16 g mol⁻¹ = 62.5 mol. The mole ratio CH₄ : CO₂ is 1 : 1, so moles CO₂ = 62.5 mol. Mass of CO₂ = 62.5 mol × 44 g mol⁻¹ = 2750 g = 2.75 kg. Explanation: the carbon in methane from fossil fuels was locked away for millions of years; burning it moves that carbon into the atmosphere faster than the carbon cycle removes it, so atmospheric CO₂ rises. CO₂ absorbs infrared radiation emitted by the Earth and traps heat, which enhances the greenhouse effect. Methane is also a greenhouse gas.

questions.prompt: Explain how burning hydrocarbon fuels can harm human health. Refer to two pollutants and give an equation for the formation of one of them.
questions.model: Carbon monoxide is formed by incomplete combustion, e.g. 2CH₄(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO(g) + 4H₂O(l). It binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen, so the blood carries less oxygen. Particulate matter, such as PM2.5 soot particles, is breathed deep into the lungs and is linked to asthma, lung disease and heart disease. Nitrogen oxides form when N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g) at the high temperatures in engines; NO₂ irritates the lungs, and sulfur dioxide from sulfur impurities irritates the airways.
